justifications.clinical.clinicalOutcomes: High-repetition training enabled; not superior to matched conventional OT in Cochrane review.
justifications.clinical.efficiency: Device-specific manufacturer training; requires institutional access to robotic upper limb system.
justifications.clinical.caseloadApplicability: Limited by expensive robotic equipment access; applicable only at select research or specialty centers.
justifications.clinical.reimbursement: Very limited insurance coverage; mostly research or cash-pay; some commercial payers beginning to consider coverage.
justifications.clinical.marketDemand: Limited employer demand; primarily academic stroke centers and research hospitals.
justifications.clinical.patientSatisfaction: Novel technology appeals; some prefer conventional hands-on OT.
justifications.healthTech.industryPlacement: Bionik (InMotion), Tyromotion, and Kinarm hire clinical specialists.
justifications.healthTech.vendorDemand: Small vendor ecosystem with steady clinical-specialist demand.
justifications.healthTech.salaryPremium: Modest premium aligned with rehab robotics roles.
justifications.healthTech.technicalSkillDepth: Direct work with sensor-instrumented robotic devices builds device literacy.
justifications.healthTech.transitionFit: Defined pathway into upper-limb robotics vendor roles.
justifications.business.cashPayViability: Intensive neuro-recovery and stroke programs successfully sell robotic UE training as cash-pay packages.
justifications.business.pricingLeverage: Tech novelty and visible equipment support premium pricing in neuro-recovery clinics.
justifications.business.marketDifferentiation: Few clinics own UE robotics, creating clear visual and marketing differentiation.
justifications.business.ownerLeverage: Once equipment is in place, mid-level clinicians can deliver protocols; moderately scalable beyond the owner.
justifications.business.marketDemand: Stroke and SCI consumers searching for 'robotic therapy' is a growing but still small segment.
justifications.business.efficiency: Capital cost of robots ($50k-$300k) is the big barrier; the training itself is brief.
justifications.academicClinical.facultyRecognition: Useful signal of tech-forward neuro expertise but not a recognized credential for promotion.
justifications.academicClinical.scholarship: Robotic rehab is an active research area with NIH funding and many publications.
justifications.academicClinical.teachingValue: Increasingly relevant in neuro curricula as students expect exposure to rehab technology.
justifications.academicClinical.evidenceDepth: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses exist; effect sizes are modest but the literature is solid.
justifications.academicClinical.facultyDemand: Not commonly required in faculty job ads outside research-intensive programs.
justifications.academicClinical.efficiency: Vendor training is short and cheap relative to traditional credentialing pathways.
